title: Mishpatim: the heart of a stranger (Exodus 23:9)
hookLine: "for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers"

lines: THE FIRST DAY, HOLDING YOUR TRAY.
cards: Remember a first day: a new school, a new city, a new country. You don't know where the bathroom is, or which jokes are allowed.
You stand at the edge of a group, holding your tray, trying not to look like you're looking for a seat. Almost everyone has felt that at least once. Most of us forget it as soon as we belong.
The Torah, in the middle of laws about courts and bribes and fair judgment, asks the Israelites not to forget it.

teach.h: A STRANGER SHALT THOU NOT OPPRESS.
teach.b: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And a stranger shalt thou not oppress; for ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

The Hebrew for stranger is ger, from a root meaning to sojourn, to live somewhere that isn't originally yours. Abraham calls himself a ger when he buys a grave for Sarah: a stranger and a sojourner among the locals.
Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, ger also came to mean a convert to Judaism, someone who chose to join the people.
But here, in Exodus, it means the outsider living among you: the immigrant, the foreigner, the one without family or land to protect them. And look at the reason given. Not because it's the law.
Not because God says so, though God does. Because you know.
The Hebrew says you know the nefesh of the stranger, the soul, the inner life. You've been the one at the edge, the one without rights. Use that memory.
The Talmud counts how often this comes up: one sage says the Torah warns about the stranger in thirty-six places; others say forty-six.

Either way, few commands are repeated so often. Even in this portion it's the second time; a chapter earlier, the same warning appears. It seems the Torah expected people to forget, and kept reminding them.

how: Jewish communities often cite the command to love and protect the stranger when welcoming newcomers and immigrants, and the memory of being strangers in Egypt is retold every year at the Passover seder.

o: a stranger: an outsider who lives among you
a servant: a worker bound for six years
an enemy: someone who harms the people

games.q: inside the word ger — tap the pairs.

s: the verse's reason is simply that God commands it
the reason given is memory: you know the stranger's heart, for you were strangers.
the Talmud counts dozens of warnings about the stranger
one sage says thirty-six; others say forty-six.
in Exodus, ger mainly means a convert
here it means the outsider living among you; the convert sense came later.

games.q: the Torah wants you to protect the stranger. what reason does the verse give?
o: strangers might become powerful one day.
you know the stranger's heart: you were strangers in Egypt.
it will bring you good luck.
games.why: memory. you know the stranger's nefesh, their inner life, because you lived it.

practice: Bring back a time you were the new one: a school, a job, a country, a family you married into. Notice where you didn't know where to stand, and who, if anyone, made room for you.
Then think of someone new in your life now, at work, on your street, in your community, and what would have helped you then.

wordCard.voice: Ger. The stranger, the one who sojourns among you. And the Torah's reason for kindness to them: you were strangers too.

orig.note: Hebrew: stranger, sojourner; later also a convert to Judaism.

carryVoice: Your line: you know the stranger's heart. Memory can be a kind of kindness. Until tomorrow.
